description:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

We're a team taking on this year's challenge: building an interactive trainer that lets young learners experience what it really takes to run a lunar or Martian outpost.
summary:
We've developed a web-app that allows the user to find places on Earth with similar attributes to given places in the Moon and Mars.

Powered by open data from NASA and other space agencies (links below), Terra Vista speeds up R&D by bringing the harsh environments of our planetary neighbors Down to Earth—giving teams a practical place to test equipment and run simulations before leaving the planet.

Because every mission has different goals, Terra Vista prioritizes certain environmental factors over others depending on what you are testing. For example, searching for water beneath the ice focuses heavily on mean temperature and ground reflectivity.

Beyond the raw science, Terra Vista also accounts for real-world realities on the ground. It flags geopolitical conflict zones and strictly protected areas—like North Sentinel Island in India—so teams aren't sent to places they can't safely or legally visit.
details: Terra Vista asks a practical question: where on Earth can we rehearse a specific Moon or Mars mission? We start from real field campaigns run by NASA and ESA, such as suited moonwalks on volcanic ground, rovers on sand, drilling into ground ice and working under a low Sun. We turn each one into surface conditions that NASA data can measure, then score all land on Earth against a real target like the lunar south pole or Jezero crater. The method is checked against sites agencies already use. It then suggests new regions and says plainly what is similar, how much, and where the analogy breaks. Planners get a shortlist with sources that shows what each site can and cannot test. What makes it creative is that it starts from a mission instead of a planet, and that it is honest about its limits: every value cites its source. We built it with NASA Earth, Moon and Mars datasets, Google Earth Engine, Python and a mobile-first Next.js/three.js web app, with help from SI (Claude Code). Along the way we weighed scientific validity, what Earth can never reproduce (gravity, vacuum), logistics and access, and ease of use.
